newsitem.title: GERMANY: Krupp, Thyssen confirm steel venture.
newsitem.headline: Krupp, Thyssen confirm steel venture.

text.p: German steel giants Krupp Hoesch and Thyssen AG said late on Wednesday that they had signed a basic agreement of understanding on founding a joint steel-producing company.
Confirming earlier statements from the companies individually, the statement said Thyssen would take a 60 percent stake in the new firm while Krupp would take a 40 percent share.

According to the statement, the accord avoids forced layoffs and is the best possible solution to ensure the future of Dortmund, at the heart of Germany's troubled steel-making Ruhr region, as an industrial centre.

Thyssen AG said it would announce details of the tie-up at a news conference on Thursday. Wednesday's compromise defused the hostile takeover bid that Fried. Krupp AG Hoesch-Krupp had was launched last week.
The joint statement said the two companies were confident the new venture would create a market-leading steel company.

Although the statement did not mention specific job losses, Ekkehard Schulz, chairman of Thyssen Stahl AG, said earlier that the new company will have a workforce of some 18,000 employees, compared to a combined workforce of 26,000 now.

The steel merger would take four years to complete and would create a producer with an annual capacity of 15 million tonnes of crude steel, putting it third in Europe behind British Steel and France's Usinor-Sacilor.
Of the estimated 8,000 jobs to be cut, nearly 4,000 would come from Krupp Hoesch Stahl operations, mainly in Dortmund where its blast furnace operations will be closed, Schulz said.

"Workforce reductions will definitely be carried out with social compensation," Hans-Wilhelm Grasshoff, chairman of steel unit Krupp Hoesch Stahl, had said in an earlier statement. "We rule out any forced layoffs under this steel plan."

Schulz said: "The costs that arise by ruling out forced layoffs must not be borne by the new company or by Thyssen," a clear indication that Thyssen would make Krupp pay for its unwanted takeover bid.
Deutsche Bank AG, meanwhile, remained defiant after receiving heavy public criticism of its role in the aborted hostile takeover.
Deutsche's presence on the boards of both Krupp and Thyssen raised questions about the scale of its influence in the takeover proceedings.
"We don't think our image has been damaged, seen professionally," Deutsche chief executive Hilmar Kopper said.

Wolfgang Clement, economics minister in the state of North Rhine-Westphalia, told reporters the two companies would invest up to 1 billion marks ($593 million) in Krupp's Dortmund steel works, countering fears that it might be closed down.
He said Krupp and Thyssen had pledged to create around 1,300 jobs in Dortmund in other areas to limit the total number of jobs that would be lost in the city.
The investment would transform Dortmund from a steel-producing plant to a processing plant with new, modern galvanising, joining and cold-rolling facilities.

The two companies' steelworks remained at a standstill on Wednesday after unions vowed to fight the creation of the joint venture. Workers threatened to strike for as long as it takes the two companies to hammer out details of the merger.
Harald Schartau, head of the North Rhine-Westphalia unit of the powerful steel and engineering union IG Metall, said the union would provide "massive resistance" to the job cuts.
Thyssen Stahl's Schulz told around 5,000 steel workers in Duisburg that job cuts would be made through offering early retirement and natural wastage over a period of four years. ($1=1.6868 Mark)
